# Machine Learning Foundations

### From Explanation to Generalizable Prediction

**Chapter 11 · From Data to Thesis**

Dr. Polla Fattah

---

## Two Cultures of Data Analysis

In 2001, statistician Leo Breiman published a landmark paper: *"Statistical Modeling: The Two Cultures"*.

Until now in this course, we have lived in the **Inference & Explanation Culture**:
- We asked: *"Does sleep statistically influence GPA after controlling for stress?"*
- We judged models by **$p$-values, confidence intervals, and theoretical interpretability**.
- We focused on **unbiased parameter estimation** ($\hat{\beta}$).

Now, we cross the frontier into the **Predictive Machine Learning Culture**:
- We ask: *"Can we accurately identify which incoming students will drop out before it happens?"*
- We judge models by one criterion only: **How accurately do they predict on data they have never seen?**

---

## Prediction vs. Explanation: Side by Side

| Dimension | Explanation (Chapters 7–10) | Prediction (Chapters 11–16) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Guiding Question** | *Why* did this outcome happen? | *What* will happen for a new case? |
| **Evaluation Metric** | $p$-values, effect sizes, adjusted $R^2$ | Out-of-sample ROC-AUC, RMSE, F1 |
| **Model Structure** | Parsimonious, causally interpretable | Any architecture that generalizes well |
| **Primary Hazard** | Confounding, omitted variable bias | **Overfitting**, data leakage |
| **Data Usage** | Fit to 100% of historical sample | Strict **Train / Validation / Test** split |

> A model can be a brilliant explainer yet a terrible predictor.  
> Conversely, a powerful predictor may offer zero causal explanation.

---

## Research Question 9: Early Dropout Detection

The university leadership approaches Elaf's research team with an urgent operational challenge:

> **Research Question 9 (Predictive Risk)**:  
> *"Can we build a predictive model using data available at the end of Semester 1 to identify students at high risk of considering dropout, so targeted academic and counseling support can be deployed before Year 2?"*

- **The Stakes**: Intervening early saves degrees; missing an at-risk student leads to unaddressed crisis.
- **The Constraint**: The model can *only* use data available at the end of Semester 1. Anything later is illegal **data leakage**!

---

# Generalization & Overfitting

---

## What is Generalization?

Any real dataset is composed of two distinct components:

$$\text{Observed Data} = \text{Underlying True Pattern (Signal)} + \text{Sample Noise}$$

- The **Signal** is the true, repeatable law of nature (e.g., higher chronic stress elevates dropout risk).
- The **Noise** is the accidental idiosyncrasy of the specific sample (e.g., student #42 was bitten by a dog on survey day).

> **A model generalises when it learns the signal and ignores the noise.**  
> A model **overfits** when it mistakes the noise for the signal!

---

## Visualizing the Spectrum: Underfitting vs. Overfitting

Let us simulate a simple wave: $y = \sin(2x) + \epsilon$ with 15 training points:

```
    Underfitting (High Bias)            Good Fit (Balanced)             Overfitting (High Variance)
          Degree 1 (Linear)               Degree 3 (Cubic)                  Degree 12 (Wiggly)
          
          ^                               ^                               ^     *
          │      *     *                  │      *     *                  │    / \   *
          │    *   *                      │    /¯ \  *                    │   /   \ / \ *
          │  *       *                    │  /     \                      │  *     V   \
          │─────────────────>             │/─────────\──────>             │─────────────\───>
          Too rigid to see wave!          Captures true wave!             Chases every random dot!
```

---

## Simulating Overfitting in R

Let us run this exact simulation:

```r
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

true_curve  <- function(x) sin(2 * x)
make_points <- function(n) {
  x <- runif(n, 0, 3)
  tibble(x = x, y = true_curve(x) + rnorm(n, sd = 0.3))
}

set.seed(3)
train_points <- make_points(15)  # 15 training points
new_points   <- make_points(300) # 300 unseen test points from same generator
```

We fit three polynomial models:
- **Degree 1**: Straight line (`lm(y ~ x)`)
- **Degree 3**: Gentle curve (`lm(y ~ poly(x, 3))`)
- **Degree 12**: Ultra-flexible curve (`lm(y ~ poly(x, 12))`)

---

## The Simulation Results

```r
rmse <- function(actual, pred) sqrt(mean((actual - pred)^2))

# Model Evaluation Comparison:
# Degree 1 (Linear):     Train RMSE = 0.54 | Test RMSE = 0.58
# Degree 3 (Cubic):      Train RMSE = 0.28 | Test RMSE = 0.31  <-- Optimal Generalization!
# Degree 12 (Complex):   Train RMSE = 0.08 | Test RMSE = 2.45  <-- Severe Overfitting!
```

Look at Degree 12:
- On its **training data**, it looks miraculous ($\text{RMSE} = 0.08$, nearly zero error!).
- On **new data**, it explodes ($\text{RMSE} = 2.45$, eight times worse than the straight line!).

> **Training error is a dangerous illusion.**  
> The more complex the model, the better it fits its own training data, and the worse it performs in the real world!

---

## The Bias-Variance Tradeoff

Every predictive model faces an inescapable mathematical tension:

$$\text{Expected Test MSE} = \text{Bias}^2 + \text{Variance} + \text{Irreducible Noise } \sigma^2$$

```
   Prediction Error
         ^                                    Total Test Error (U-Shape)
         │  \                                /
         │   \                              /      / Variance (Rises with complexity)
         │    \                            /      /
         │     \                          /      /
         │      \___________*____________/______/
         │       \                      /
         │        \  Optimal Model     /
         │         \                  /
         │          \________________/__________> Bias^2 (Falls with complexity)
         └───────────────────────────────────────> Model Flexibility / Complexity
```

- **Bias**: Error from erroneous assumptions (underfitting; missing the real signal).
- **Variance**: Error from sensitivity to small fluctuations in training data (overfitting).

---

# Designing a Fair Test: The Tidymodels Framework

---

## The Tidymodels Philosophy

In modern R, the standard ecosystem for machine learning is **`tidymodels`** (developed by Max Kuhn and the Posit team):

```
                     The Tidymodels Modular Ecosystem
                     
     [ rsample ]     Data Splitting (Train/Test) & Cross-Validation Folds
          │
          ▼
     [ recipes ]     Preprocessing, Imputation, Dummy Coding, Normalization
          │
          ▼
     [ parsnip ]     Unified Model Specification (consistent API across engines)
          │
          ▼
    [ workflows ]    Glues Recipe + Model Specification into one pipeline
          │
          ▼
      [ tune ]       Hyperparameter Grid Search & Bayesian Optimization
          │
          ▼
    [ yardstick ]    Performance Metrics (ROC-AUC, Accuracy, Precision, Recall)
```

```r
library(tidymodels)
tidymodels_prefer() # Resolves namespace conflicts in favor of tidymodels
```

---

## The Machine Learning Pipeline

```
                     ┌───────────────────────────────┐
                     │       All Raw Data (N)        │
                     └───────────────┬───────────────┘
                                     │
                    initial_split() (75% / 25%)
                     ┌───────────────┴───────────────┐
                     ▼                               ▼
       ┌───────────────────────────┐   ┌───────────────────────────┐
       │     Training Set (75%)    │   │      Test Set (25%)       │
       └─────────────┬─────────────┘   │   (Locked in a safe!      │
                     │                 │    Never seen during      │
      vfold_cv() (10 Folds)            │    model development)     │
                     ▼                 │                           │
       ┌───────────────────────────┐   │                           │
       │ Recipe + Model Tuning     │   │                           │
       │ Select Best Hyperparam    │   │                           │
       └─────────────┬─────────────┘   │                           │
                     │                 │                           │
          last_fit() │                 │                           │
                     └─────────────────┼───────────────────────────┘
                                       ▼
                       ┌───────────────────────────────┐
                       │ One-Time Final Evaluation     │
                       │   (Honest Real-World Metric)  │
                       └───────────────────────────────┘
```

---

# Data Preparation & Preventing Data Leakage

---

## Assembling the Semester 1 Dataset

We assemble our prediction dataset strictly using variables known at the end of Semester 1:

```r
# 1. Questionnaire scores computed at Year 1 orientation
scores <- questionnaire |>
  mutate(
    stress_4     = 6 - stress_4,
    stress       = rowMeans(pick(stress_1:stress_6), na.rm = TRUE),
    burnout      = rowMeans(pick(burnout_1:burnout_6), na.rm = TRUE),
    support      = rowMeans(pick(support_1:support_6), na.rm = TRUE),
    satisfaction = rowMeans(pick(satisfaction_1:satisfaction_4), na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  select(student_id, stress, burnout, support, satisfaction)

# 2. Link student demographics + Semester 1 performance records
dropout_data <- students |>
  left_join(scores, join_by(student_id)) |>
  left_join(semesters |> filter(semester == 1) |> select(-semester), join_by(student_id)) |>
  mutate(considering_dropout = factor(considering_dropout, levels = c("Yes", "No"))) |>
  select(-student_id, -supervisor_id, -workshop, -workshop_sessions)
```

---

## Beware of Data Leakage!

Why did we explicitly remove `workshop` and `workshop_sessions`?

```r
select(-student_id, -supervisor_id, -workshop, -workshop_sessions)
```

- The wellbeing workshop took place in **Semester 2**.
- If we include Semester 2 variables in a model designed to run at the **end of Semester 1**, we have committed **Temporal Data Leakage**!
- Data leakage gives the model information from the future that will not be available in real deployment.

> **Rule**: If a variable does not exist at the exact moment of decision, it must NOT enter the predictive model!

---

## The Target Variable: Class Imbalance

Let us inspect the distribution of our outcome variable `considering_dropout`:

```r
dropout_data |> count(considering_dropout) |> mutate(Share = round(n / sum(n), 3))
```

```
  considering_dropout   n Share
1 Yes                  88 0.147
2 No                  512 0.853
```

- Only **14.7%** of students consider dropping out ("Yes").
- **85.3%** do not ("No").
- This is an **Imbalanced Classification Problem**.
- As we will see, class imbalance makes standard accuracy completely useless!

---

# Data Splitting & Preprocessing Recipes

---

## Splitting with `rsample`

We split our data: 75% for model training, 25% locked away for testing:

```r
set.seed(2026)

# Stratify by considering_dropout to guarantee 14.7% "Yes" in both splits!
dropout_split <- initial_split(
  dropout_data, 
  prop = 0.75, 
  strata = considering_dropout
)

dropout_train <- training(dropout_split) # 450 students
dropout_test  <- testing(dropout_split)  # 150 students
```

Why is `strata = considering_dropout` essential?
- If we split purely at random, rare "Yes" cases might accidentally clump into the test set, starving the training algorithm of positive examples.

---

## Building a Preprocessing `recipe`

A `recipe` specifies the step-by-step transformations needed before data enters a machine learning algorithm:

```r
dropout_recipe <- recipe(considering_dropout ~ ., data = dropout_train) |>
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())
```

What each step executes:
1. `step_impute_median`: Replaces missing numeric values with the predictor's median.
2. `step_dummy`: Converts factors (`faculty`, `gender`) into $0/1$ binary columns.
3. `step_normalize`: Converts all numeric variables to $z$-scores ($\text{mean} = 0, SD = 1$).

---

## The Leak-Free Preprocessing Rule

```
                                  TRAINING SET
                                       │
                      Calculate Median, Mean, SD
                                       │
                     ┌─────────────────┴─────────────────┐
                     ▼                                   ▼
             Transform Train Set                 Transform Test Set
             (Using Train Stats)                 (Using Train Stats!)
```

> **Critical Principle**:  
> The medians, means, and standard deviations used to normalize the data are computed **from the training set only**!

If you compute the mean across all 600 students before splitting, test set information leaks into your training preprocessing. `recipes` handles this automatically and safely.

---

# Model Specification with `parsnip` & `workflows`

---

## Model Specification with `parsnip`

In standard R, every package has its own idiosyncratic syntax:
- `glm(..., family = binomial)`
- `randomForest(..., ntree = 500)`
- `e1071::svm(..., kernel = "radial")`

`parsnip` standardizes model definitions into three clean components:
1. **Type**: What kind of model? (`logistic_reg()`, `decision_tree()`)
2. **Mode**: `classification` or `regression`?
3. **Engine**: Which R package executes it? (`set_engine("glm")`)

```r
logistic_spec <- logistic_reg() |>
  set_engine("glm") |>
  set_mode("classification")
```

---

## Bundling with `workflows`

A `workflow` packages your preprocessing recipe and your model specification into a single, cohesive bundle:

```r
logistic_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(dropout_recipe) |>
  add_model(logistic_spec)

# Fit workflow on training data in one step:
logistic_fit <- fit(logistic_wf, data = dropout_train)
```

When you call `fit(logistic_wf)`:
1. It trains the recipe on `dropout_train`.
2. It bakes `dropout_train`.
3. It fits the logistic regression model on the baked data.
4. It remembers all transformation parameters for future test predictions!

---

# Classifier Evaluation: The Accuracy Paradox & ROC-AUC

---

## Generating Predictions with `augment()`

We test the trained model on our unseen `dropout_test` set:

```r
test_results <- augment(logistic_fit, new_data = dropout_test)

test_results |> 
  select(considering_dropout, .pred_class, .pred_Yes, .pred_No) |> 
  head(4)
```

```
  considering_dropout .pred_class .pred_Yes .pred_No
1 No                  No              0.042    0.958
2 Yes                 Yes             0.781    0.219
3 No                  No              0.115    0.885
4 No                  No              0.038    0.962
```

- `.pred_class`: The hard categorical classification (using standard 0.50 cutoff).
- `.pred_Yes`: The predicted continuous probability of considering dropout.

---

## The Accuracy Paradox

Let us calculate overall classification accuracy using `yardstick`:

```r
test_results |> accuracy(truth = considering_dropout, estimate = .pred_class)
```

```
.metric  .estimator .estimate
accuracy binary         0.867
```

**86.7% Accuracy sounds impressive!**  
... But look at what happens if we build a "Lazy Model" that simply predicts "No" for every student:

```r
mean(dropout_test$considering_dropout == "No")
# [1] 0.853 (85.3% Accuracy!)
```

> **The Accuracy Paradox**:  
> A completely useless model that predicts "No" for everyone achieves **85.3% accuracy**, but catches **0%** of at-risk students!  
> For imbalanced data, **accuracy is a dangerously deceptive metric.**

---

## The Confusion Matrix

To understand classifier performance, we inspect the **Confusion Matrix**:

```r
conf_mat(test_results, truth = considering_dropout, estimate = .pred_class)
```

```
          Truth
Prediction Yes  No
       Yes  14   7   <-- 14 True Positives (Caught!), 7 False Alarms
       No    8 121   <-- 8 False Negatives (Missed!), 121 True Negatives
```

Key Diagnostic Ratios:
- **Sensitivity (Recall)**: $\frac{TP}{TP + FN} = \frac{14}{22} = \mathbf{63.6\%}$ (Share of at-risk students successfully detected).
- **Specificity**: $\frac{TN}{TN + FP} = \frac{121}{128} = \mathbf{94.5\%}$ (Share of safe students correctly left alone).
- **Precision (PPV)**: $\frac{TP}{TP + FP} = \frac{14}{21} = \mathbf{66.7\%}$ (When flagged, probability student is truly at-risk).

---

## The ROC Curve & ROC-AUC

Instead of evaluating a single arbitrary cutoff ($0.50$), the **Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC)** curve plots Sensitivity vs. (1 - Specificity) across **all possible probability thresholds**:

```
    Sensitivity (True Positive Rate)
        1.0 ^              /¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯\
            │            /           \   <-- High AUC (e.g., 0.88)
            │          /
            │        /
            │      /                     <-- Diagonal Line: AUC = 0.50
            │    /                           (Completely Random Guessing!)
            │  /
            │/─────────────────────────> 
            0.0                       1.0   (1 - Specificity) [False Positive Rate]
```

- **ROC-AUC (Area Under the Curve)**:
  - Measures the probability that the model ranks a randomly chosen at-risk student higher than a safe student.
  - $\text{AUC} = 0.50$: Pure random coin flip.
  - $\text{AUC} \ge 0.80$: **Good discriminative ability**.
  - **Invariant to class imbalance!**

---

## Calculating Test ROC-AUC

```r
test_results |> roc_auc(truth = considering_dropout, .pred_Yes)
```

```
.metric .estimator .estimate
roc_auc binary         0.882
```

- **Test ROC-AUC = 0.882**:
- If we pick one random student who considered dropping out and one who did not, our Semester 1 model correctly assigns the higher risk score to the struggling student **88.2% of the time**.
- This is a highly effective, practically deployable screening tool!

---

# Demonstrating Overfitting: The 1-Nearest Neighbor Trap

---

## 1-Nearest Neighbor ($k=1$)

To prove why evaluating on training data is fatal, consider **1-Nearest Neighbor (1-NN)**:
- To predict an outcome, it searches for the single most similar student in the dataset and copies their answer.

```r
knn1_spec <- nearest_neighbor(neighbors = 1) |>
  set_engine("kknn") |>
  set_mode("classification")

knn1_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(dropout_recipe) |>
  add_model(knn1_spec)

knn1_fit <- fit(knn1_wf, data = dropout_train)
```

---

## The Illusion of Perfection

Let us test 1-NN on its **Training Data** vs. its **Test Data**:

```r
# Evaluated on Training Data:
augment(knn1_fit, new_data = dropout_train) |> 
  roc_auc(considering_dropout, .pred_Yes)
# [1] 1.0000000  <-- "PERFECT" AUC OF 1.0!

# Evaluated on Unseen Test Data:
augment(knn1_fit, new_data = dropout_test) |> 
  roc_auc(considering_dropout, .pred_Yes)
# [1] 0.6481250  <-- Collapses to 0.65!
```

- On training data, every student's nearest neighbor is *themselves*, so it achieves 100% accuracy and an AUC of 1.0.
- On test data, it collapses to near-worthless performance ($\text{AUC} = 0.65$).
- It memorized the noise without learning the pattern!

---

# Resampling with V-Fold Cross-Validation

---

## The Dilemma: How to Compare Models Honestly?

- We need to choose between algorithms (Logistic Regression vs Decision Trees vs Random Forests).
- We need to select tuning settings (e.g., how deep should a decision tree be?).
- **The Catch**: We cannot use the training data (rewards overfitting), and we **must not touch the test set** (that burns our one-time final exam!).

> **The Solution**: **$V$-Fold Cross-Validation** (resampling the training set).

---

## How 10-Fold Cross-Validation Works

We partition the training set (450 students) into 10 equal folds (45 students each):

```
Round 1:  [ Train on Folds 2 to 10 (405 students) ]  ──>  [ Evaluate on Fold 1 (45) ]
Round 2:  [ Train on Folds 1, 3 to 10 (405 students)] ──>  [ Evaluate on Fold 2 (45) ]
Round 3:  [ Train on Folds 1 to 2, 4 to 10 (405)    ] ──>  [ Evaluate on Fold 3 (45) ]
...
Round 10: [ Train on Folds 1 to 9 (405 students)   ]  ──>  [ Evaluate on Fold 10 (45) ]

Average the 10 evaluation scores ──> Honest Out-of-Sample Performance Estimate!
```

Every single training student is used for evaluation exactly once, by a model that **never saw them during training**!

---

## Running Cross-Validation in R

```r
set.seed(2026)

# Create 10 stratified cross-validation folds
dropout_folds <- vfold_cv(dropout_train, v = 10, strata = considering_dropout)

# Evaluate logistic regression workflow across all 10 folds
logistic_cv <- fit_resamples(
  logistic_wf, 
  resamples = dropout_folds,
  metrics = metric_set(roc_auc, accuracy)
)

collect_metrics(logistic_cv)
```

```
.metric  .estimator  mean     n std_err
accuracy binary     0.858    10 0.0142
roc_auc  binary     0.871    10 0.0215
```

- **Cross-validated AUC = 0.871 ($\pm 0.02$)**:
- We obtain an honest estimate of real-world generalization without ever touching the test set!

---

# Hyperparameter Tuning with `tune_grid`

---

## Parameters vs. Hyperparameters

| Type | Definition | How It Is Determined | Examples |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Model Parameter** | Internal weights learned directly from data | Optimized during `fit()` via MLE or OLS | Regression $\beta_0, \beta_1$, Tree branch splits |
| **Hyperparameter** | Structural setting governing model flexibility | **Tuned** by researcher using cross-validation | Tree depth ($D$), Neighbors ($k$), Penalty ($\lambda$) |

---

## Decision Trees: Tuning `tree_depth`

A **Decision Tree** partitions data by asking a sequence of binary questions (e.g., *"Is stress > 3.4?"* $\rightarrow$ *"Is support < 2.1?"*).

- A tree of **Depth 1** (one question) is too simple $\rightarrow$ **High Bias (Underfitting)**.
- A tree of **Depth 10** (10 questions deep) memorizes individual students $\rightarrow$ **High Variance (Overfitting)**.

```r
# Mark tree_depth for tuning with tune()
tree_spec <- decision_tree(
  tree_depth = tune(), 
  min_n = 10, 
  cost_complexity = 0
) |>
set_engine("rpart") |>
set_mode("classification")

tree_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(dropout_recipe) |>
  add_model(tree_spec)
```

---

## Executing the Grid Search

We test depths from 1 to 10 across our 10 cross-validation folds:

```r
set.seed(2026)
tree_tuning <- tune_grid(
  tree_wf,
  resamples = dropout_folds,
  grid = tibble(tree_depth = 1:10),
  metrics = metric_set(roc_auc)
)

# Visualize the tuning curve
autoplot(tree_tuning) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  labs(
    title = "Cross-Validated ROC-AUC Across Tree Depths",
    x = "Tree Depth (Flexibility)",
    y = "10-Fold CV ROC-AUC"
  )
```

---

## Interpreting the Tuning Curve

```
      ROC-AUC
        0.85 ^                 * Peak: Depth 3 (AUC = 0.82)
             │                / \
        0.80 │               /   \______* Depth 5 (AUC = 0.79)
             │              /            \
        0.70 │             /              \____* Depth 10 (AUC = 0.74, Overfitting!)
             │            /
        0.50 │  * Depth 1 (Underfitting)
             └───────────────────────────────────────> Tree Depth
```

- Depth 1 (Stump): AUC $\approx 0.62$ (Too simple).
- **Depth 3**: Peaks at $\text{AUC} \approx \mathbf{0.824}$ (Sweet spot!).
- Depths 5–10: Performance degrades back down to $0.74$ as the tree overfits training noise.

```r
best_depth <- select_best(tree_tuning, metric = "roc_auc")
best_depth
# # A tibble: 1 x 2
#   tree_depth .config             
#        <int> <chr>               
# 1          3 Preprocessor1_Model03
```

---

# The Final Test: `last_fit()` & Model Comparison

---

## Finalizing the Workflow & The Test Set Exam

Now that our hyperparameter is chosen, we unlock the test set:

1. `finalize_workflow()`: Injects `tree_depth = 3` into the tree workflow.
2. `last_fit()`: Fits the finalized workflow on the **entire 75% training set**, and evaluates it **once on the 25% test set**:

```r
final_tree <- tree_wf |>
  finalize_workflow(best_depth) |>
  last_fit(dropout_split, metrics = metric_set(roc_auc, accuracy))

collect_metrics(final_tree)
```

```
.metric  .estimator .estimate
accuracy binary         0.840
roc_auc  binary         0.815
```

---

## The Head-to-Head Showdown

We also evaluate our baseline Logistic Regression on the exact same test set:

```r
final_logistic <- last_fit(
  logistic_wf, 
  dropout_split, 
  metrics = metric_set(roc_auc, accuracy)
)

collect_metrics(final_logistic)
```

```
.metric  .estimator .estimate
accuracy binary         0.867
roc_auc  binary         0.882
```

| Model Architecture | 10-Fold CV AUC | Test Set ROC-AUC | Test Accuracy |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **Tuned Decision Tree ($D=3$)** | 0.824 | 0.815 | 84.0% |
| **Simple Logistic Regression** | **0.871** | **0.882** | **86.7%** |

---

## Occam's Razor in Machine Learning

Why did a simple 200-year-old logistic regression outperform a modern machine learning decision tree?

1. **Nature of the Data Generating Process**:
   - In student psychology, dropout risk increases **smoothly and continuously** with stress and lack of support.
   - Logistic regression models smooth, linear log-odds surfaces.
   - Decision trees slice feature space into rigid, orthogonal rectangular boxes, struggling with smooth additive relationships.
2. **Sample Size Constraints**:
   - With $N = 450$ training rows, flexible non-parametric algorithms struggle to estimate high-dimensional partitions reliably.

> **Golden Rule of Applied Machine Learning**:  
> Always establish a linear baseline (e.g., Logistic Regression). Make complex algorithms *earn* their place by demonstrably beating the baseline!

---

# Case Study: Financial Risk Scoring (`credit_data`)

---

## Universal Transferability of Tidymodels

The exact same workflow translates seamlessly to banking, credit risk, or healthcare:

```r
data(credit_data, package = "modeldata")

set.seed(1)
credit_split <- initial_split(credit_data, strata = Status)

# Recipe handles missing numbers (median) and missing categories (mode)
credit_recipe <- recipe(Status ~ ., data = training(credit_split)) |>
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_impute_mode(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())

credit_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(credit_recipe) |>
  add_model(logistic_reg())

last_fit(credit_wf, credit_split) |> collect_metrics()
```

- Whether predicting student dropout, hospital readmission, or mortgage default: **the workflow structure is identical.**

# Ethical Considerations in Predictive Modeling

---

## Algorithmic Fairness & Human Impact

Predictive models deployed on human beings have profound ethical consequences:

1. **The Cost of Errors is Asymmetric**:
   - **False Positive** (Flagging a safe student as at-risk): Minor advisor check-in; minimal harm.
   - **False Negative** (Failing to detect a struggling student): Student drops out unassisted; catastrophic harm!
2. **Algorithmic Bias**:
   - A model with 0.88 AUC overall may have 0.92 AUC for majority students but only 0.65 AUC for international or minority students.
   - Always audit performance across demographic subgroups (`faculty`, `gender`, `mode`).
3. **Purpose of Modeling**:
   - Early warning models must be used **constructively to offer supportive resources**, never punitively (e.g., to withhold funding).

# Thesis Checkpoint: Reporting Machine Learning Results

---

## How to Report ML in an Academic Thesis (Methods)

> *"To address Research Question 9 regarding the early identification of students at risk of dropout, a supervised classification framework was developed using the tidymodels ecosystem in R. The analytical sample was restricted to predictors available at the conclusion of Semester 1 to prevent temporal data leakage. The dataset (N = 600) was partitioned into a 75% training set (n = 450) and a 25% holdout test set (n = 150), stratified by dropout consideration.*
>
> *Within the training set, feature preprocessing included median imputation for missing numerical predictors, one-hot dummy coding for categorical factors, and z-score standardization. Model selection and hyperparameter optimization were performed using 10-fold stratified cross-validation. Candidate architectures included penalized logistic regression, k-nearest neighbors, and decision trees tuned across tree depths from 1 to 10.*
>
> *Final performance was quantified using the Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (ROC-AUC) on the untouched holdout test set."*

---

## How to Report ML in an Academic Thesis (Results)

> *"Cross-validation results indicated that logistic regression achieved the highest generalization performance (CV ROC-AUC = .871, SE = .021), outperforming the optimized decision tree (depth = 3, CV ROC-AUC = .824, SE = .026). When evaluated on the holdout test set, the logistic regression model maintained high discriminative accuracy (ROC-AUC = .882, Sensitivity = .636, Specificity = .945, Accuracy = 86.7%), markedly exceeding the baseline no-information rate (85.3%).*
>
> *Substantively, the model demonstrated that psychological survey metrics (elevated academic burnout and low supervisor support) measured at matriculation, combined with Semester 1 GPA, provide sufficient predictive signal to reliably flag at-risk candidates three semesters prior to potential attrition."*

---

## Chapter 11 Summary: Core Principles

1. **Prediction vs Inference**: Predictive models are judged solely on unseen data. High $R^2$ or low $p$-values on training data mean nothing out-of-sample.
2. **The Bias-Variance Tradeoff**: Complex models overfit by memorizing sample noise; simple models underfit by missing the signal.
3. **No Peeking**: The test set is locked away immediately; preprocessing statistics (means, medians) must derive strictly from training data.
4. **Prevent Leakage**: Exclude any variable occurring after the moment of prediction (e.g., Semester 2 workshops).
5. **Beware Accuracy**: For imbalanced classes, raw accuracy is deceptive. Use ROC-AUC, sensitivity, specificity, and precision.
6. **Cross-Validation**: 10-fold CV provides an honest out-of-sample performance estimate for model comparison without touching the test set.
7. **Occam's Razor**: Linear models often beat complex machine learning algorithms on smooth psychological and social phenomena.
